statements.quote: The GPU does the matrix math; but *something* has to decide which GPU runs which layer, when to move data between memory and disk, how a process that has run for a week keeps from corrupting its neighbor, and how a line of Python becomes a billion instructions on a specific chip.

statements.quote: It is deliberately broader than a “history of Unix” or a “top ten programming languages.” It covers the operating systems you will rarely hear named (GM-NAA I/O, Multics, VMS, Plan 9, the Hurd, BeOS), the languages that shaped how we *think* about computation (Lisp, ALGOL, Smalltalk, Prolog, APL), the tools that made it possible to *maintain* software complex enough to be useful (compilers, `make`, version control), and the people and ideas — their rivalries, their ideologies, their stubbornness — that decided which abstractions survived.
statements.section: Software: The Layer That Made Everything Else Possible

statements.quote: Because the single most important fact about software is not technical: it is that software was built by **rival minds competing over the shape of thought itself**, and without that competition there is no stack, and no AI on top of it.

statements.section: Multics (1964–1969): The “Too Much” System

statements.quote: It was the engineering ideal of the age — *comprehensiveness, correctness, a single perfect whole*.
statements.section: Multics (1964–1969): The “Too Much” System

statements.quote: It was also, to the people on the team, a kind of art project, and the team culture (the “games” they built to test the graphics, the long dinners, the sense of building a cathedral) was real \cite{multics_plan9}.
statements.section: Multics (1964–1969): The “Too Much” System

statements.quote: When it failed, it did not fail for lack of brilliance; it failed for the sin of **scale**.
statements.section: Multics (1964–1969): The “Too Much” System

statements.quote: The lesson — *that a small, composable, imperfect system can beat a large, perfect, monolithic one* — became the founding creed of the Unix camp, and the argument has not been settled since.
statements.section: Multics (1964–1969): The “Too Much” System

statements.quote: The Multics team did not just build a file system; they built a *culture*.
statements.section: Multics (1964–1969): The “Too Much” System

statements.quote: To test the (then cutting-edge) display and input capabilities of their terminals, they wrote games.
statements.section: Multics (1964–1969): The “Too Much” System

statements.quote: One of them, **Space Travel**, was a simple space-shooter, and it is the direct ancestor of the first “video game” to run on a time-sharing system.
statements.section: Multics (1964–1969): The “Too Much” System

statements.quote: The crucial detail for our story: **Space Travel** was written by **Ken Thompson** and a colleague *as a game*, but when the Multics graphics were too slow and the hardware too costly to keep iterating on, Thompson took the game home and rewrote it on a cheap, discarded **PDP-7** that was sitting in a corner \cite{multics_plan9}.
statements.section: Multics (1964–1969): The “Too Much” System

statements.quote: The operating system he wrote *around that game* to make it run — with its file system, its shell, its little kernel — is what became Unix.
statements.section: Multics (1964–1969): The “Too Much” System

statements.quote: The most influential operating system in history was, in a very real sense, **a side project born from a game that the “serious” operating system was too slow to run**.
statements.section: Multics (1964–1969): The “Too Much” System

statements.quote: **Unix** was written at **Bell Labs** starting in **1969**, by **Ken Thompson** and (from about 1971) **Dennis Ritchie**, on that spare PDP-7 \cite{unix_ts}.
statements.section: Unix and the Hacker Ethos (1969–1973)

statements.quote: Its name was a playful jab at Multics — a seven-letter pun, and a statement of intent: *the opposite of that over-engineered thing*.
statements.section: Unix and the Hacker Ethos (1969–1973)

statements.quote: Its first kernel fit on a single page of documentation.
statements.section: Unix and the Hacker Ethos (1969–1973)

statements.quote: It had a file system, a shell (a command interpreter, the first “sh,” written by Thompson himself), a few utilities, and — crucially — an attitude.
statements.section: Unix and the Hacker Ethos (1969–1973)

statements.quote: The attitude was later codified as the **Unix philosophy**, and it is an *ideology* as much as a technical style:
statements.section: Unix and the Hacker Ethos (1969–1973)

statements.quote: * **Do one thing, and do it well.** A program should be a small, sharp tool.
statements.section: Unix and the Hacker Ethos (1969–1973)

statements.quote: * **Build tools that work together.** Write programs that can be *combined*, piping the output of one into the input of another.
statements.section: Unix and the Hacker Ethos (1969–1973)

statements.quote: * **Text is universal.** Represent everything as plain text, so any tool can read any other tool's output.
statements.section: Unix and the Hacker Ethos (1969–1973)

statements.quote: The **pipe** — the `|` operator that connects the output of one program to the input of another — was added in **1973** by **Doug McIlroy**, and it is arguably the single most important idea in the design: it is the “level of indirection” made concrete.
statements.section: Unix and the Hacker Ethos (1969–1973)

statements.quote: You do not need to know what the two programs do to each other; you only need to know they share a *vocabulary* (text) and a *contract* (one reads stdin, the other writes stdout).
statements.section: Unix and the Hacker Ethos (1969–1973)

statements.quote: This is composition, and composition is the entire game \cite{unix_ts}.
statements.section: Unix and the Hacker Ethos (1969–1973)

statements.quote: Unix began in a language called **B** (1969, Thompson's own invention, a tiny precursor).
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: In **1972**, **Dennis Ritchie** extended B into **C**, and in **1973** he and Thompson did something that had never been done: they **rewrote the operating system in the very language the operating system was compiling** \cite{unix_ts}.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: Before C, an operating system was written in the machine's own assembly language, which meant it was *locked to one machine*; to run it on a different computer you had to rewrite it from scratch.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: After C, the Unix kernel was **portable**: compile the same C source on a different machine and you get a working Unix for that machine.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: This is a quiet, enormous deal, and it is worth stating plainly, because it is the *direct* ancestor of everything about modern software, including AI.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: **C made software relocatable.** It is the reason a “library” can be built once and used on a thousand machines.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: It is the reason the next 50 years of software — the compilers, the databases, the browsers, the GPUs' drivers, the frameworks, and the machine-learning libraries (NumPy, cuDNN, PyTorch's kernels) — could be *shared* rather than *rewritten*.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: The entire modern software economy rests on the assumption that a piece of code, written once, will run on many machines.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: That assumption is a 1973 Bell Labs decision \cite{unix_ts}.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: The psychology of C is the psychology of the Unix group in a nutshell: **pragmatism over elegance, and smallness over power.** C is famously *bare*: it has almost no error checking, no object system, no “safety” — it gives you exactly the machine and nothing more.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: Purists of other languages have long mocked it (“C is not a high-level language; it is *portable assembly*”), and the mocking is half right.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: But that bareness is the *feature*.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: C is “assembly that you can take with you,” and it is the reason the *same* low-level performance you get from writing to the metal is also the language you use to build the *infrastructure* on top of which everything else runs.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: When a machine-learning framework needs to squeeze the last flop out of a GPU, it descends to C and CUDA; the high-level Python on top is the *interface*, and C (and the assembly it lowers to) is the *work*.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: When asked, years later, to describe the feeling of writing Unix, the members of the Bell Labs group gave a one-word answer that has become a kind of password for the hacker identity: **“Glory.”** The joke was that the motivation for the work was not the paycheck (Bell Labs was a research lab, not a product company) and not the users (there were barely any), but the *satisfaction of the thing working*.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: Unix was built because building a clean, small, composable system was *fun*, and the fun was the point \cite{bell_labs}.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: This is the seed of the **hacker ethic** — the belief that the intrinsic pleasure of making a clever, working thing is a legitimate, even primary, motivation — and it is a motivation that has powered most of the “open” side of software ever since.
statements.section: C: The Operating System, Rewritten to Be Portable (1972)

statements.quote: A portable, powerful, well-liked operating system was, commercially, a *dangerous* thing for AT&T, because Bell Labs (part of AT&T) was not allowed to *sell* Unix.
statements.section: The Unix Wars, and the Idea of a Standard (1979–1990)

statements.quote: Universities and vendors began shipping their own versions, and within a decade there were two incompatible families: the **Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD)**, out of the University of California, Berkeley (which added the socket interface for networking and the famous `csh` and `tcpdump`), and **System V**, AT&T's commercial line \cite{unix_ts}.
statements.section: The Unix Wars, and the Idea of a Standard (1979–1990)

statements.quote: They were *Unixes* in the cultural sense but *incompatible* in the technical one — a program written for one often would not run on the other.
statements.section: The Unix Wars, and the Idea of a Standard (1979–1990)

statements.quote: The response was **POSIX** (Portable Operating System Interface), a set of standards published in the 1980s that defined a *common* Unix: the same system calls, the same command-line tools, the same shell semantics, on every machine \cite{unix_ts}.
statements.section: The Unix Wars, and the Idea of a Standard (1979–1990)

statements.quote: POSIX is one of the first big acts of *standardization* in software, and it is a small miracle that it worked at all, because standardization is the natural enemy of the Unix hacker ethos (which prefers to *invent* the next tool rather than agree on one).
statements.section: The Unix Wars, and the Idea of a Standard (1979–1990)

statements.quote: The tension — **open invention versus agreed standard** — is the tension that runs through all of software, and it is a tension we will see again, and again, in the languages and in the open-source movement.
statements.section: The Unix Wars, and the Idea of a Standard (1979–1990)

statements.quote: The “wars” were also, and this is the part that belongs in the psychology, a **war of identities**.
statements.section: The Unix Wars, and the Idea of a Standard (1979–1990)

statements.quote: The BSD camp was *academic and free* (they gave the code away); the System V camp was *commercial and closed* (you bought a license).
statements.section: The Unix Wars, and the Idea of a Standard (1979–1990)

statements.quote: The same two poles — *open and academic* versus *closed and commercial* — that produced the Unix wars went on to produce the entire modern map of the software industry, from the free-software movement to the proprietary empires, from open-source Linux to the walled gardens.
statements.section: The Unix Wars, and the Idea of a Standard (1979–1990)

statements.quote: The operating system was the first battleground, and the battle never really ended; it just changed fronts.
statements.section: The Unix Wars, and the Idea of a Standard (1979–1990)

statements.quote: In the early 1990s, some of the original Unix people at Bell Labs — Thompson, **Rob Pike**, and a few others — did what purists do when the original idea has, in their view, been corrupted by decades of add-ons: they **started over from scratch** \cite{multics_plan9}.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: The result was **Plan 9 from Bell Labs** (often just “Plan 9,” a reference to Ed Wood's 1957 cult science-fiction film *Plan 9 from Outer Space*).
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: Plan 9 took the Unix idea — *“everything is a file”* — and pushed it to its logical extreme.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: In Unix, files, devices, and (later, via sockets) network connections were given a *file-like* interface.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: In Plan 9, *everything* was a file: a window on your screen, a device, a process, a connection to a machine across the network — all addressed the same way, through the same small set of operations, over a single, simple protocol called **9P** \cite{plan9_9front}.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: The idea was radical **simplicity**: one idea, applied uniformly, instead of a dozen special cases.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: A program on one machine could open a file on another machine with exactly the same call it used to open a local file.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: Plan 9 was, like Multics before it, *ahead of its time* and never commercially successful \cite{multics_plan9}.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: But it is beloved by exactly the kind of people who love it, and its descendants are alive today.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: The community that keeps it going (and a cleaner reimplementation called **9front**) maintains it as a working system and as a *philosophical statement* \cite{plan9_9front}.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: And in **1995**, the same group began **Inferno**, a system with its own **virtual machine** and its own high-level language, **Limbo** (a safe, garbage-collected successor to C), aimed at *embedded* and *media* applications \cite{plan9_9front}.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: Inferno's most visible (and, to its fans, most delightful) feature was its color: the whole user interface, the windows, the text, everything, was rendered in **blue** — a deliberate, almost aesthetic choice that made an Inferno machine unmistakable at a glance \cite{plan9_9front}.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: The story of Plan 9/Inferno is a caution and a compliment at once.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: It is a **compliment** to the Unix people: they could, and did, take their own idea to its purest form and make it *work*, and in doing so they produced one of the most elegant operating-system designs ever conceived.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: It is a **caution** because it shows the cost of that purity: a system so clean and so “correct” that the rest of the world, busy building incompatible things, simply drove past it.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: The “one true operating system” is a beautiful idea and a doomed product, and the people who built it knew it; they built it anyway, because building it *was* the point.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: The “9” in Plan 9 is a Bell Labs in-joke, but not the one often told.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: The name is a reference to **Ed Wood's 1957 cult science-fiction film *Plan 9 from Outer Space*** — widely called one of the worst films ever made, which is exactly the self-deprecating register the Bell Labs group enjoyed \cite{plan9_9front}.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: (It is *not* named for a hypothetical “ninth edition” of Unix: Research Unix had already reached an actual **9th edition** in 1986.) The number nine then recurs through the project as a running motif — the protocol is **9P**, the implementation **9front**, the tape format **9tape** — part humor, part a quiet cult around a single, lucky, arbitrary number.
statements.section: Plan 9 and Inferno: The “Start Over” Operating System (1990s–2000s)

statements.quote: By the mid-1970s, the microprocessor made a *whole computer* cheap enough to fit on a desk, and with the personal computer came the first *consumer* operating-system war.
statements.section: The Personal Computer and the Operating-System War (1974–1995)

statements.quote: The first popular microcomputer operating system was **CP/M** (Control Program/Monitor), written in 1974 by **Gary Kildall** at **Digital Research** for the 8-bit Intel 8080.
statements.section: CP/M: The First Microcomputer OS (1974)

statements.quote: It was the dominant OS on many 8080/Z80 machines (on the Apple II it required a Z-80 card), and it defined, in miniature, the model that followed: a tiny kernel, a disk file system (the `.COM`, `.EXE`, `.SYS` file types still echo it), and a command line \cite{chm}.
statements.section: CP/M: The First Microcomputer OS (1974)

statements.quote: The story of CP/M meeting IBM is one of the great “what-ifs” of the industry.
statements.section: CP/M: The First Microcomputer OS (1974)

statements.quote: In 1980, IBM was designing its first personal computer and needed an operating system.
statements.section: CP/M: The First Microcomputer OS (1974)

statements.quote: It approached Digital Research about **CP/M-86**, a 16-bit version.
statements.section: CP/M: The First Microcomputer OS (1974)

statements.quote: The famous (and fiercely disputed) anecdote has Kildall unavailable for the key meeting because he was water-skiing, and an IBM engineer walking away and instead talking to **Microsoft** \cite{chm}.
statements.section: CP/M: The First Microcomputer OS (1974)

statements.quote: Whether or not the water-skiing is literally true, the *consequence* is not in dispute: IBM licensed its PC's operating system from Microsoft, not from CP/M's author.
statements.section: CP/M: The First Microcomputer OS (1974)

statements.quote: The result made Microsoft, and it made the next twenty years of computing.
statements.section: CP/M: The First Microcomputer OS (1974)

statements.quote: What Microsoft sold to IBM was not, at first, even a serious operating system.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: In 1980, **Tim Paterson** at the tiny firm **Seattle Computer Products** had written **86-DOS** — internally nicknamed **QDOS**, *Quick and Dirty Operating System* — a quick clone of CP/M ported to the new 16-bit Intel 8086, built in about six weeks and left thin and unfinished \cite{chm}.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: When the IBM deal came together in 1981, Microsoft **hired Paterson** and **bought 86-DOS** (version 1.10) for a reported **twenty-five thousand dollars**, reworked it, renamed it **MS-DOS**, and licensed it to IBM, which shipped it as **PC DOS** \cite{chm}.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: The **IBM PC**, released in August 1981, used it.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: Two decisions in that contract shaped the industry.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: First, Microsoft kept the *rights* to the OS and licensed it to *other* manufacturers as well, not just IBM — a small clause that turned MS-DOS into the OS of the *entire* PC market, not just IBM's.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: Second, IBM did **not** patent its **BIOS** (the basic firmware that boots the machine), so others could *clean-room* reverse-engineer it and build “PC-compatible” clones, from Compaq up \cite{chm}.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: The result was the **Wintel** standard: Intel's CPU plus Microsoft's OS, cloned by everyone, the dominant platform of the personal-computer era, and the platform on which the first wave of consumer software — and, later, the first wave of desktop AI tools — was built \cite{windows_ms}.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: It is a detail that is easy to miss and worth stating, because it is the difference between a product and a *bet*: at the time Microsoft licensed DOS to IBM, **DOS was not the company's main product**.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: Microsoft's first product was **Altair BASIC** (1975, written by Bill Gates and Paul Allen for the first personal computer kit), and the company's center of gravity was on software for the emerging PC as a *market*, not on the operating system.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: DOS was a quick, cheap acquisition to *have* an OS to hand to IBM; it was meant to be the *hook*, not the *prize* \cite{chm}.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: The fact that the hook became the most profitable piece of software in the history of the world is one of the great ironies, and it is a pure function of *timing and positioning* rather than of technical superiority — MS-DOS was, by any engineering measure, a *worse* operating system than the alternatives on the market.
statements.section: MS-DOS and the IBM PC (1981)

statements.quote: The most instructive operating-system failure of the PC era was not a failure of technology but a **failure of trust**.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: In the mid-1980s, **IBM and Microsoft** decided to build a *real* 32-bit operating system *together*, a successor to DOS that could do preemptive multitasking, protected memory, and a proper graphical interface.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: The result was **OS/2**, released in 1987 \cite{windows_ms}.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: For a time it looked like the future.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: OS/2 was, technically, a *better* operating system than the DOS that was about to dominate: it was 32-bit, it had true preemptive multitasking, it had a real memory model, and its **Presentation Manager** GUI was ahead of its time \cite{windows_ms}.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: And then the two partners pulled in opposite directions.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: **IBM** decided OS/2 was *the* future and went all-in on it, building the powerful **OS/2 Warp** (1994).
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: **Microsoft**, meanwhile, did something far simpler and far more effective: it bolted a graphical shell, **Windows 3.0** (1990), *on top of the existing DOS*, and let it run on the *huge* installed base of cheap PCs that OS/2 did not.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: Windows was, engineering-wise, a patch on a 16-bit machine; but it was *cheap, familiar, and already installed*, and it won \cite{windows_ms}.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: The fallout was a long, bitter legal and commercial dispute that ran through the 1990s, and it is a case study in how a *technically superior* system loses to a *strategically positioned* one.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: OS/2 Warp was a good, fast, solid operating system that sold to almost no one, and it is remembered mainly as the *near-miss* — the OS that, had its two creators pulled in the same direction, might have been the Windows we all use.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: The lesson belongs in the psychology: the operating-system business was never decided by the *best* kernel.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: It was decided by **distribution, backward compatibility, and the willingness of one partner to do something the other had not authorized**.
statements.section: OS/2: The Collaboration That Ate Itself (1987)

statements.quote: **Windows 1.0** (1985) was a graphical shell over DOS; it was useful but fragile.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: **Windows 3.0** (1990) and **3.1** (1992) made it *good* — a real graphical environment, VGA color, the file manager and the programs people actually wanted — and they made the PC a mass-market machine \cite{windows_ms}.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: But under the hood it was still DOS, 16-bit, and the engineers at Microsoft knew it was a *temporary* structure.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: So, in parallel, Microsoft built a *real* operating system from the ground up: **Windows NT** (1993), the “New Technology” kernel.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: The decisive move was hiring **Dave Cutler**, the architect of VMS at **Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC)**, and a small team of some of the best systems engineers in the industry, to write it \cite{windows_ms}.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: NT was 32-bit, preemptive, portable across several CPUs, and *secure* in a way DOS and its Windows shell never were.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: It was the “serious” Microsoft operating system, and it is the direct ancestor of every modern Windows (and of the security model of much of the server world).
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: The strange, telling fact is that for a *decade* Microsoft ran **two** operating systems in parallel: the *popular* one (Windows 95, 98, ME — still DOS at its core) and the *serious* one (NT, 2000, XP — the real kernel).
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: **Windows 95** (1995) was the cultural event: the Start button, the graphical shell, plug-and-play, and a launch that was a genuine moment in consumer technology \cite{windows_ms}.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: It was, technically, the *lesser* of the two; it won on *familiarity and price*.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: The two lines finally merged in **Windows XP** (2001), which put the *popular* Windows shell on the *serious* NT kernel.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: The modern Windows — and, through it, the platform that a huge share of the world's AI software was first written and tested on — is the *descendant of that 1993 bet by a small team* \cite{windows_ms}.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: The operating-system war of the 1980s did not end with the Wintel standard; it simply moved *up* a layer, into the **browser**.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: In the mid-1990s, **Netscape** (Netscape Navigator) and **Microsoft** (Internet Explorer) fought a ferocious, industry-defining fight for the default browser, a fight that was really a fight for *the new front door to the computer* \cite{windows_ms}.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: Microsoft's move — bundling the browser *with* the operating system — was so decisive, and so legally controversial, that it became the core of the first great antitrust case against a software company.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: The pattern is identical to the OS/2 story: the *better* product did not win; the product that was *already there*, that *cost nothing*, that the user did not have to think about, did.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: And the *idea* that was born in that war — that the *browser* is the new universal application platform, the new “operating system” of the internet — is the idea that made the *web* a place where software (including, eventually, web-based AI tools) could run *anywhere*, without installation.
statements.section: Windows and NT: The Kernel Built by a Small Team of the Best (1985–1995)

statements.quote: Unix, Windows, and their war are the famous thread.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: But the space was crowded, and several *other* operating systems made contributions that are easy to skip and hard to replace.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: * **VAX/VMS (1977, DEC).** Digital Equipment Corporation's VMS was the “Swiss Army knife” of the 1980s: a powerful, preemptive, multi-user operating system with *excellent* security, virtual memory, and fault tolerance, running on the VAX minicomputer \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: It was the default on a huge number of scientific and commercial sites, and its *security model* (mandatory access control, the idea that the *system* — not the user — enforces who can read what) influenced the security design of systems that followed.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The psychology of VMS is the psychology of DEC: a company that built *machines* for the people who actually *used* computers, in a culture that prized *reliability* over *elegance* \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: * **Mach (1985, CMU) and the microkernel.** At Carnegie Mellon, **Avie Tevanian** (and a team) built **Mach**, a **microkernel** — an operating system in which the *kernel* is deliberately *tiny* (only the absolute minimum: scheduling, basic memory, basic I/O), and everything else (file systems, device drivers, the network) runs *outside* it, in user space \cite{mach}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The argument was that a small, simple, *verifiable* core is easier to get *right* than a large, monolithic kernel, and that everything else can be *replaced* without touching the core.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: This set off a famous, decades-long debate — the **microkernel versus the monolithic kernel** argument — between the purists (who wanted the clean microkernel) and the pragmatists (who said the monolith is *faster* and the “clean” version is a *theoretical* nicety).
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The debate was played out publicly, in print, in the mid-1980s, and it has never been fully settled \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: Mach matters because it did not die in a journal.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: It became the *kernel* of **NeXTSTEP** (1989), the operating system of **Steve Jobs's** NeXT computer, which combined the Mach microkernel with a **BSD** user space and an **object-oriented** system built around **Objective-C** \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: NeXTSTEP had a beautiful, consistent graphical interface (later **Aqua**) and a *modern* object model, and when Apple bought NeXT in 1997, NeXTSTEP became the foundation of **macOS** (and, with it, of **iOS**).
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: So the microkernel that a CMU team built as a *research* kernel is, today, the *basis of the operating system on a billion phones* \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The “pure” research idea won — not by being *chosen*, but by being *bought*.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The **Tanenbaum–Torvalds debate** — **Andrew Tanenbaum** defending the **microkernel** (his teaching OS, MINIX) against **Linus Torvalds**, who chose a **monolithic** kernel for **Linux** — is one of the great public arguments in operating-systems history, and it is worth reading for what it reveals about how engineers *disagree*: after years of arguing that a small, clean core was the road to a *reliable* OS, Tanenbaum publicly dismissed Torvalds’s monolithic Linux as a *dead end* “not suitable for teaching,” while Torvalds and his camp retorted that a monolith is *simpler, faster, and actually buildable* \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: Both sides were *brilliant* and *right*, about different things.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The microkernel people were right that a small core is *easier to verify and harder to crash*; the monolith people were right that the *extra context switches* in a microkernel make it *slower* for the common case.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The resolution that history arrived at is a *hybrid*: a *small* core, with the *most performance-critical* pieces (the file system, the network) *pulled back inside* it.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: Modern kernels — including the Linux kernel and the kernel of the Mac — are, in practice, *monoliths that learned a little from the microkernel*, and the argument is a perfect example of a *technical* debate that is really an *aesthetic* one: do you value *clean correctness* or *measured speed*?
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: * **GNU Hurd (1991, the free operating system).** **Richard Stallman**'s **GNU** project set out to build a *complete, free* operating system — one whose every part could be studied, copied, and modified.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The kernel of that system, the **Hurd** (HURD, a name that is its own backronym), was built on top of Mach \cite{gnu_hurd}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The Hurd is famous for one thing above all: it has been *“almost done”* for decades.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The phrase “the GNU Hurd will be done, and then it will be free” became a running, affectionate joke in the free-software world — *done* in the sense of “functioning,” but never in the sense of “the default thing people actually run” \cite{gnu_hurd}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The Hurd is a monument to an *idea* (a completely free, user-controlled system) that outran its *execution*, and it is the flag of the **free-software** movement, for which the *freedom* of the software is the point, not the *convenience* \cite{gnu_hurd}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: * **Amiga OS (1985, Commodore).** The Amiga was the machine that *should have* eaten the world.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: Running on a Motorola 68000, its operating system offered, in **1985**, **preemptive multitasking**, a true **graphical user interface** (Intuition), and a multi-channel audio system, on a *consumer* machine that cost less than the business computers of the day \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: It was the platform of a generation of computer musicians and demoscene artists, and its OS was, for its price class, *years* ahead.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: It failed for *business* reasons (Commodore's management, not the technology), and it is remembered as the great *what-if* of the home computer: a *real* multitasking graphical OS, in a living room, before the IBM PC had one \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: founded 1990, and the media-oriented computer).** **Be Inc.** (founded in 1990 by **Jean-Louis Gassée**, who had been a senior executive at Apple) built an operating system explicitly aimed at *multimedia*: a fast, preemptive, threaded design that treated *media* — video, audio, the user interface — as first-class citizens, and that could run a 3-D “Media Transport” in real time \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: Be never became a mass-market OS, and the company's assets were eventually acquired by **Palm, Inc.** (2001) primarily for its *people* and its *code*.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: BeOS is a reminder that the operating-system space was never a two-horse race; it was a *bazaar* of visions, each one a different answer to “what is a computer *for*?” — for Be, the answer was *media*, and for a moment it looked like the right answer for the coming web \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: * **MINIX (1987, the teaching operating system).** **Andrew Tanenbaum** wrote **MINIX** with a deliberately different goal: not to be the *best* operating system, but to be the *smallest one you can actually teach* \cite{minix3}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: It was small enough that a student could *read the entire kernel* in a semester, and he used it to argue his side of the microkernel debate (MINIX 3 became a true microkernel) \cite{minix3}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: Its importance is *educational*: for a generation, MINIX was the *textbook* operating system, the one students actually *read* and *modified*, and the people who learned to think about kernels by reading MINIX went on to build the real ones \cite{minix3}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The most dramatic proof that an operating-system bug can *ground a spacecraft* is the **Mars Pathfinder** (1997).
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The lander ran on **VxWorks**, a real-time operating system, and a few minutes after touchdown it *lost contact* — a failure that was traced, in a now-classic post-mortem, to a **priority-inversion** bug, a flaw in how the OS *ordered* the tasks it was running.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: A *low*-priority task held a lock that a *high*-priority task needed, and a *medium*-priority task jumped in line, so the high-priority task (which had to watch the lander's systems) was *starved* — a textbook real-time failure, caused by an *off-the-shelf* OS feature that had not been configured for the worst case \cite{mars_pathfinder}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The fix — a **priority-inheritance** mutex, a well-known, cheap, *textbook* correction — would have prevented it.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: The story is told in every real-time operating-system course as the ultimate argument for *boring, correct, conservative* operating-system design: the most sophisticated software on Mars was defeated not by the physics of Mars, but by a *scheduling bug in the software that managed the software*.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: And the rest, briefly, so the map is complete: **RISC OS** (Acorn, the clean, elegant OS of the ARM microcomputer); **QNX** (the *embedded* operating system that, quietly, runs in a large share of the cars, medical devices, and industrial controllers around the world — the OS you *never* see because it is *inside* things); **pSOS** (a real-time operating system for embedded systems, created around 1982 by Alfred Chao); **Xenix** (Microsoft's Unix, before the company found its destiny in Windows); and **SCO UNIX** (one of the many “Unixes” of the wars).
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: Each was a different answer to the same question, and each left a scar on the design of the systems that survived \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Other Operating Systems (the “and so on and so forth”)

statements.quote: If the operating system is the *machine that manages itself*, the programming language is the *way a human talks to it*.
statements.section: Programming Languages: The Development of a Way of Thinking

statements.quote: And the history of programming languages is, more than any other part of software, a history of *ideas about thinking*: what is a *computation*?
statements.section: Programming Languages: The Development of a Way of Thinking

statements.quote: which abstractions are *honest* and which are *lies*?
statements.section: Programming Languages: The Development of a Way of Thinking

statements.quote: Each major language is a *thesis*, and the “winning” language of an era is the thesis that most people found *bearable*.
statements.section: Programming Languages: The Development of a Way of Thinking

statements.quote: The languages were not invented in the order we use them.
statements.section: Programming Languages: The Development of a Way of Thinking

statements.quote: They were invented in the order of *ambition*: first to *save the labor of coding* (FORTRAN), then to *express mathematics* (Lisp, ALGOL), then to *build systems* (C), then to *build objects* (Simula, Smalltalk, C++), then to *build anything* (the modern polyglot era).
statements.section: Programming Languages: The Development of a Way of Thinking

statements.quote: The first high-level language was not *elegant*; it was *economic*.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: In 1957, a team at IBM led by **John Backus** built **FORTRAN** (FORmula TRANslation), the first language that let a *scientist* write a calculation in a form close to the *mathematics* (a sum, a loop, a formula) instead of in machine code \cite{fortran2}.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: The claim that sold it — that a FORTRAN program ran as fast as, or faster than, hand-tuned assembly, while taking a fraction of the time to *write* — was, for the first time, *credible* \cite{fortran2}.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: FORTRAN is *still* the language of a huge amount of scientific and numerical computing; the *computational kernel* of much of modern numerical software is, literally, FORTRAN, wrapped in newer languages.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: In the same era, **Grace Hopper**'s group at the Navy was doing the other half of the revolution: *compilation* itself.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: Hopper's **A-0** system (1952) was the **first compiler** — a program that *translated* a high-level language into machine code automatically, instead of the programmer writing the machine code by hand \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: Hopper *coined the word “compiler”* and, more importantly, she *preached the idea* that programming should be *independent of the machine*: that a person should write for *the problem*, not for *this particular computer*.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: That is the entire philosophy of high-level programming in one sentence, and it is the reason we can write Python on a machine that did not exist when we learned it \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: Hopper's **FLOW-MATIC** (1959), a business language with an *English-like* syntax, became the basis of **COBOL** (1959), the language of *bookkeeping*, which — and this is a fact that surprises people — is *still* running a large share of the world's banking and insurance systems, half a century on \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: Grace Hopper is one of the great *translators* in the history of the field, in both senses.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: She built the *first compiler*, but she also *translated the idea of the computer* from “a machine for people who can read its guts” into “a tool for people who can state a problem” \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: Her insistence that the language should be *close to English* (“why should the computer speak a language only its builder understands?”) was a *sociological* insight as much as a technical one: the *limiting* resource was not the machine, it was the *number of people who could program it*, and the only way to get more programmers was to make the language *bearable to non-specialists* \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: That insight — *that the value of a language is the size of the set of people who can use it* — is the insight behind BASIC, Python, and, in a different way, behind the *natural-language* interface of modern AI.
statements.section: The First Languages (1950s): Saving the Labor of Coding

statements.quote: In **1958**, **John McCarthy** at MIT invented **Lisp** (LISt Processing), and it was a *different kind of thing* from FORTRAN.
statements.section: Lisp (1958): The Language That Treated Computation as Mathematics

statements.quote: Where FORTRAN was a language for *numbers*, Lisp was a language for *symbols* and *functions*, built directly on the **lambda calculus** of **Alonzo Church** (1930s) — the mathematical theory of *functions as first-class objects*.
statements.section: Lisp (1958): The Language That Treated Computation as Mathematics

statements.quote: In Lisp, a *function* is a *value*: you can pass it around, return it, build new functions out of old ones.
statements.section: Lisp (1958): The Language That Treated Computation as Mathematics

statements.quote: The whole language is, essentially, a small *calculus*, and it was the first language that treated *computation itself* as a *mathematical object* to be manipulated \cite{lispworks}.
statements.section: Lisp (1958): The Language That Treated Computation as Mathematics

statements.quote: Lisp invented or popularized a stack of ideas that are now *everywhere* but whose origins are in 1958: the **automatic garbage collector** (1959, the memory that cleans itself up, so the programmer never has to free it), the *first-class function*, the *recursive* definition, and the *dynamic* type \cite{lispworks}.
statements.section: Lisp (1958): The Language That Treated Computation as Mathematics

statements.quote: And it created a *culture*: the MIT **Lisp machine** (a computer designed from the ground up to run Lisp) and the **hacker** subculture that grew up around it, for whom the *pleasure* of the language — its *elegance*, its *power*, its “way of thinking” — was the point, not the *application*.
statements.section: Lisp (1958): The Language That Treated Computation as Mathematics

statements.quote: The psychology of Lisp is the psychology of **McCarthy**, who was, by all accounts, *magnificent and difficult*.
statements.section: Lisp (1958): The Language That Treated Computation as Mathematics

statements.quote: In 1959, in an essay, he predicted that *within a decade* computers would be as intelligent as human beings — a prediction that was *spectacularly* wrong about the *date* and has, in a sense, been *spectacularly* right about the *event*, some six decades later \cite{lispworks}.
statements.section: Lisp (1958): The Language That Treated Computation as Mathematics

statements.quote: The *idea* that a machine could *think*, stated by a *logician* in 1959 as a *matter of course* (“of course we will, it is just engineering”), is one of the founding intuitions of artificial intelligence, and Lisp is the language in which that intuition was first *programmed*.
statements.section: Lisp (1958): The Language That Treated Computation as Mathematics

statements.quote: If Lisp was the *mathematical* language, **ALGOL** (ALGOrithmic Language: ALGOL 58, the **ALGOL 60** report of 1960, and its revised report of 1963) was the *structured* one \cite{algol60}.
statements.section: ALGOL (1958/1960): The Language That Taught Us *Structure*

statements.quote: ALGOL was designed by a committee with a *deliberate* goal: to make programming *readable* and *correct*, by giving the language a real *structure*.
statements.section: ALGOL (1958/1960): The Language That Taught Us *Structure*

statements.quote: It introduced, or consolidated, the ideas that every “structured” language since has inherited: **block structure** (a program is a tree of *blocks*, each with its own *scope*), **lexical scoping** (a variable is visible in exactly the block where it is defined and the blocks nested inside it), and **structured control** (`if`, `for`, `while`) \cite{algol60}.
statements.section: ALGOL (1958/1960): The Language That Taught Us *Structure*

statements.quote: ALGOL's deepest contribution was a *theorem*, proved in 1966 by **Böhm and Jacopini**: that *any* computable program can be written using just *three* control structures — *sequence*, *if*, and *while* — with no `goto` at all \cite{goto_harmful}.
statements.section: ALGOL (1958/1960): The Language That Taught Us *Structure*

statements.quote: That result turned the *style* of programming into a *mathematical* question, and it set the stage for the most famous essay in the history of software.
statements.section: ALGOL (1958/1960): The Language That Taught Us *Structure*

statements.quote: In **1968**, **Edsger Dijkstra** wrote, to a friend, the letter that became **“Go to Statement Considered Harmful”** \cite{goto_harmful}.
statements.section: ALGOL (1958/1960): The Language That Taught Us *Structure*

statements.quote: The argument was *small* and *enormous* at once: the `goto` (the unconditional jump, the “go to line 47”) was not merely *ugly*; it was *dangerous*, because it let a program's *control flow* become a *spaghetti* that no human could *follow*, and a program no human can follow is a program no human can *prove correct*.
statements.section: ALGOL (1958/1960): The Language That Taught Us *Structure*

statements.quote: The essay is a *rhetorical* masterpiece as much as a technical one, and it did what very few pieces of writing in computing have done: it *changed the way a whole profession thought about itself*, by turning *style* into *professionalism* \cite{goto_harmful}.
statements.section: ALGOL (1958/1960): The Language That Taught Us *Structure*

statements.quote: “Structured programming” — the idea that a program should have a *clean, provable* structure — is a direct child of that letter, and the *idea* that *the readability and correctness of the code is a first-class engineering concern* (not a cosmetic one) is one of the lasting contributions of the 1960s to the discipline.
statements.section: ALGOL (1958/1960): The Language That Taught Us *Structure*

statements.quote: It is also, quietly, an *AI* contribution: the insistence that a system be *understandable by a human* is the same insistence that, decades later, would drive the demand for *interpretable* and *explainable* models.
statements.section: ALGOL (1958/1960): The Language That Taught Us *Structure*

statements.quote: We met **C** (1972, Ritchie) in the Unix story; it is the *systems* language, the “portable assembly,” the language in which the operating systems, the compilers, the databases, and the *low-level* half of everything is built.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: Its standards (C89 in 1989, then C99, C11, C17, and C23) froze and extended the language that a *whole industry* had been building on \cite{unix_ts}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: **C++** is the *argument* about what C should have been.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: **Bjarne Stroustrup** at Bell Labs began in 1979 with “C with Classes” — the idea of taking the *bare* C and adding an *object model* on top of it — and it grew, over the 1980s and 1990s, into a *large* language that tries to be *everything at once*: low-level *and* object-oriented *and* generic, systems *and* application \cite{isocpp}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: C++ is *contested* in a way that few languages are — its *power* is its *complexity*, and its *complexity* is its *bug* — but it is also *indispensable*: it is the language of the *game engines*, the *browsers*, the *databases*, and a *very large* share of the *high-performance* half of machine learning (the C++ and CUDA kernels under the Python frameworks) \cite{isocpp}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: The psychology of C++ is the psychology of *refusal to choose*: it is the language for people who are not willing to give up *either* the *control* of C *or* the *convenience* of the high-level, and who are willing to pay, in *complexity*, for having both.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: * **Pascal (1970, Niklaus Wirth).** Wirth designed **Pascal** as a *teaching* language, and he *succeeded* so well that it became *the* language of the first generation of students for a decade \cite{pascal}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: Pascal took ALGOL's *structure* and made it *pedagogical*: a small, clean, *honest* language in which a student could see *exactly* what the program does.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: Wirth went on to **Modula** and **Oberon**, languages that pushed the *modular*, *small* design further, and his influence is the influence of the *idea* that a language should be *small enough to be understood* \cite{pascal}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: * **Simula (1967, Norway): the first object-oriented language.** In Norway, **Ole-Johan Dahl** and **Kristen Nygaard** built **Simula** (first Simula 67) to *simulate* real-world systems, and to do so they invented the *object*: a *thing* that bundles its *data* and its *behavior* together, and the *class* (a *template* for making many such things), and *inheritance* (one class *extends* another) \cite{chm}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: **Simula is the first object-oriented language**, and the *object* — the idea that the basic unit of a program is a *self-contained thing* that *hides* its innards and *shows* an interface — is the single most *diffused* idea in the history of programming languages.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: Every `class` in every language since, and the whole *object-oriented* paradigm (Java, C++, Python, Swift), is a *descendant* of Simula 67.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: That a *simulation* language, built to model *queues and factories*, gave the world the *object* is one of the great examples of an *idea escaping its intended use*.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: * **Smalltalk (1972, Alan Kay) and the Dynabook: the Operating System for the *Person*.** This is the single most important *side* story in the history of software for our purposes, because it is where the *computer stopped being a machine for operators and became a machine for people*.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: At **Xerox PARC**, **Alan Kay** and his team built **Smalltalk** (1972), a *pure* object-oriented language (dynamically typed, fully object-based, *no* globals), and — more importantly — they built it *on a machine with a mouse and a screen*.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: The **Xerox Alto** (1973), the *first* computer with a *graphical user interface* and a *mouse*, ran Smalltalk, and it is the *direct ancestor* of the Apple Lisa (1983) and the **Macintosh** (1984) \cite{smalltalk}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: Kay's *vision* for why he was doing all this was not “faster calculations”; it was the **Dynabook** — a concept he articulated in the late 1960s and refined for decades: a *personal* computer, *light* enough to carry, *powerful* enough to *teach a child*, with a *graphical* interface, that could be a *tool for thinking*, for *writing*, for *learning* \cite{smalltalk}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: The Dynabook is, in effect, a *1968 sketch of the tablet and the laptop and the “personal computer” and the “AI tutor” all at once*.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: It is a sketch of *exactly the kind of machine* that a modern AI assistant is trying to be: a *personal*, *graphical*, *learning* tool, *for a person*, *at the desktop*.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: The fact that the *idea* of the personal, graphical, learning computer was *stated, clearly, in 1968* — and that the *technology* (the Alto, Smalltalk) to build it *existed* in 1973 — and that it *took twenty more years* to become a product (the Mac, in 1984) is one of the great *gap* stories in the history of the field: the *idea* was there, the *prototype* was there, and the *market* was not \cite{smalltalk}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: Xerox PARC is the *Rosetta Stone* of the “ahead of its time” story.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: In the 1970s it produced, in *working form*, the *mouse*, the *graphical user interface*, *Ethernet* (the network), *laser printing*, and *object-oriented programming* (Smalltalk) — and Xerox, the company that owned it, *never shipped most of them as products* \cite{chm}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: It is also, quietly, an *AI* story: the *personal computer* that PARC imagined — a *learning*, *graphical*, *personal* tool — is the *form factor* in which modern AI *lives*.

statements.quote: * **ML, Haskell, and the pure-functional camp (1973–1990).** **ML** (1973, from the Lisp world, but *typed*) and its descendants (**Standard ML**, **OCaml**, **F#**) were built around a single, *powerful* idea: **type inference**.

statements.quote: In 1978, **Robin Milner** (with **Hindley**) showed that a program's *types* could be *figured out automatically* by the compiler, so the programmer *did not have to write them* — a *proof* about the program, done *for you*, at *compile time* \cite{haskell}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: **Haskell** (1990) pushed the *functional* idea to its *pure* limit: a *lazy* (compute only what you need, when you need it), *pure* (no side effects, the same input always gives the same output) language, in which a *function* is the *only* thing and a *program* is a *mathematical expression* \cite{haskell}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: Haskell is named for **Haskell Curry**, the logician whose work on *combinators* (and the **Curry–Howard correspondence**, the deep link between *programs* and *proofs*) is the *mathematical* foundation of the whole *typed-functional* tradition \cite{haskell}.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: The *psychology* of this camp is the *psychology of the mathematician*: the *purity* is the *point*; a *side effect* is a *sin*; a *proof* is a *program*; and the *beauty* of the *type system* is a *moral* good.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: It is the *idealist* pole of the language world, in permanent, productive *tension* with the *pragmatist* pole of C and C++.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: * **Prolog (1972, Marseille): the language of *logic*.** In France, **Alain Colmerauer** (with Philippe Roussel) invented **Prolog** (PROgramming in LOGic), a language in which you do not *tell* the computer *how* to do something; you *tell* it *what is true* (a set of *facts* and *rules*), and you *ask* it a *question*, and it *works backward* (by *logic*, by *unification* and *backtracking*) to *find* an answer \cite{prolog}.

statements.quote: Prolog was the *flagship* language of the *symbolic AI* and the *expert systems* of the 1980s, and it is the language that *most directly* embodies the *old* idea — the *Leibniz*, the *Llull*, the *Boole* idea, the idea that *reasoning* is *symbol manipulation* — that this whole course has been tracing.

statements.quote: It *lost* the argument to *statistical* methods (to the neural networks, to the “bitter lesson”), but it did not *die*; it lives on in *database* query languages, in *logic* programming, and in the *neuro-symbolic* attempt to bring *structure* back into *learning* systems \cite{prolog}.

statements.quote: * **APL (1958, Kenneth Iverson): the language of a *single notation*.** **APL** (A Programming Language) was built, by **Kenneth Iverson**, around a *single, dense, symbolic notation* — a *keyboard* of special *symbols* (the “APL keyboard”) in which an *entire* calculation could be written on *one line* \cite{apl_j}.

statements.quote: APL is *unbearable* to most people (the notation is a *barrier*) and *extraordinary* to its fans (the *conciseness* is a *superpower*), and it is the *purest* example of a language as a *notational system*: the *whole* of the language is a *notation*, and the *value* of the language *is* the *value* of the notation.

statements.quote: * **BASIC (1964, Dartmouth): the language *for everyone*.** **John Kemeny** and **Thomas Kurtz** at **Dartmouth College** invented **BASIC** (Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code) with an *explicit, almost *moral* goal: to *democratize* programming, to make it *available to people who were not specialists*, to put a *computer* in the hands of the *general student* \cite{dartmouth}.

statements.quote: BASIC is *small*, *simple*, and *forgiving*, and it was the *first* language of a *huge* number of people, from the *Altair* (where **Altair BASIC**, written by Gates and Allen, became Microsoft's *first* product) to the *home computers* of the 1980s \cite{dartmouth}.

statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: * **SQL (1974) and the relational model (1970): the language of *data*.** In 1970, **Edgar Codd** at IBM published **“A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks”** \cite{codd1970}, which proposed that *all* your data should be stored in *tables* (*relations*), and that you should *query* it with a *logical* language, not with a *program* that *navigates* the *storage*.

statements.quote: Codd won the **Turing Award** in 1981 for the *model*.
statements.section: C, C++, and the Systems Languages (1970s)

statements.quote: The *psychology* of the relational revolution is the *psychology of the *separation* of *what you want* (the *query*) from *how it is stored* (the *implementation*) — the *same* “level of indirection” that runs through the *whole* of software, applied to *data*.

statements.quote: And it is *directly* *AI*-relevant: the *relational* idea — *a clean, logical view of the data, independent of the messy storage* — is the *ancestor* of the *vector database* and the *semantic* *index* that a modern retrieval system builds.

statements.quote: * **Java (1995, Sun).** **James Gosling**'s **Java** was born from the **“Green Project”** (a *home-appliance* computer, code-named **“Oak”**) and re-tooled for the *web* as **“Write Once, Run Anywhere”** \cite{java_oracle}.

statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: * **Python (1991, Guido van Rossum): the language that *won* machine learning.** **Python** was designed, by **Guido van Rossum**, for *readability* and *pleasure*: “*Readability counts*,” “*Beautiful is better than ugly*” — the language is *explicit* in its *aesthetics*, and its *brevity* means a *program* is *shorter* and *clearer* than the *same* program in *Java* or *C++* \cite{python}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: Two facts made Python the *language* of *modern AI*.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: First, its *readability* and its *batteries-included* culture made it the *first* language a *researcher* (a *scientist*, not a *systems* *programmer*) could *use* to *prototype* an *idea* in an *afternoon* \cite{python}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: Second, the *entire* *ecosystem* of *machine-learning* tools — **NumPy**, **SciPy**, **scikit-learn**, **TensorFlow**, **PyTorch** — was *built in Python*, *on top of* C/C++/CUDA *kernels*, so that the *researcher* writes *Python* and the *machine* runs *C* \cite{python}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: Python has a *rich* *culture* of *public* *discussion* (the *mailing* *lists*, the *PEPs*, the *benevolent* *dictator*), and from that culture came a *word* that is now *used* in *every* *engineering* *shop* in the *world*: **“bikeshedding”** \cite{python}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: The *joke* is that a *committee* will *spend* *hours* *debating* the *color* of the *bicycle* *shed* (the *trivial*, *visible*, *low-stakes* *decision*) while *ignoring* the *elephant* in the *room* (the *important*, *invisible*, *high-stakes* *one*).

statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: * **JavaScript (1995, Brendan Eich): the language written in *ten days*.** **Brendan Eich** was asked, at **Netscape**, to put a *scripting* language *inside* the *browser*, and he *built* the *first* version of **JavaScript** (originally **“LiveScript”**) in *ten days* in *May 1995* \cite{javascript_mdn}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: It was, by *deliberate* *choice*, *loose* (dynamically *typed*, *forgiving*, *quick* to *write*), and it was *rebranded* **“JavaScript”** (the *Java* *name*, for *marketing*, though the *languages* are *unrelated*) \cite{javascript_mdn}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: The *irony* is *total*: a *ten-day*, *compromise*, *stopgap* language, built to *ship* a *feature*, became the *most* *deployed* programming language in the *history* of the *world*, the *language* of the *entire* *client* *side* of the *web*, and, through the **Node.js** runtime (2009), the *language* of a *huge* share of the *server* *side* as *well* \cite{javascript_mdn}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: JavaScript is the *purest* *example* of a *language* *winning* by *distribution* rather than by *design*: it is not the *best* language, by *most* *measures*, but it is the *language that is *everywhere*, and *everywhere* is a *feature*.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: * **C# (2000, Microsoft).** **Anders Hejlsberg** (the creator of *Turbo Pascal* and *Delphi*) built **C#** for Microsoft's **.NET** platform as a *synthesis*: the *syntax* and *feel* of *C++*, the *managed* *memory* and *type safety* of *Java*, the *object model* of *both* \cite{csharp_ms}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: It is the *language* of the *enterprise* and of the **.NET** ecosystem, and its *design* is a *case study* in *synthesis*: it is a language that *chose* the *best* *idea* from *each* of its *rivals* and *combined* them, and it is a *reminder* that the *history* of *languages* is a *history* of *synthesis* as *much* as of *invention*.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: * **Go (2009, Google): the *boring* language that *won*.** In 2009, **Robert Griesemer**, **Rob Pike**, and **Ken Thompson** (yes, *Ken Thompson*, the *co-creator* of *Unix* and *Plan 9*) designed **Go** at Google \cite{go_lang}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: Its *goals* were *deliberately* *anti-clever*: *fast* to *compile*, *simple* to *read*, *built-in* *concurrency* (the *goroutine*, a *lightweight* *thread*), and *no* *hidden* *complexity* \cite{go_lang}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: Go is *famous* for being *boring*, and it is *famous* for being *enormously* *successful*: it is the *language* of much of the *infrastructure* of the *cloud*, of *Docker*, of *Kubernetes*, and of a *huge* share of the *systems* that *run* the *data centers* in which *large* *models* are *trained* \cite{go_lang}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: The *psychology* of Go is the *psychology* of the *senior* *engineer* who has *seen* *enough* *clever* *languages* to *prefer* the *boring* one: *the* *best* *language* is the *one* *the whole team can read*, and *the* *best* *tool* is the *one* *that gets out of the way*.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: * **Rust (2010–2015, Graydon Hoare, Mozilla): the language that *solves* the *crash*.** **Rust** was born from a *specific* *obsession*: **memory safety**.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: A *very large* share of the *world's* *critical* *security* *vulnerabilities* come from *memory* *errors* (the *buffer* *overflow*, the *use-after-free*, the *dangling* *pointer*), and those errors live in the *low-level* languages (C, C++) that *build* the *infrastructure* \cite{rust_lang}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: Rust's answer is the **borrow checker**: a *compile-time* *proof* that *no* memory is *used* after it is *freed* and that *no* two things *write* to the *same* memory at the *same* time, *without* a *garbage* *collector* and *without* giving up *speed* \cite{rust_lang}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: Rust *refuses to compile* a program that might *crash* or *leak*, which is a *radical* *idea* (a *language* that *says no* to *your* *code*) and a *revolutionary* one (a *systems* language that is *memory-safe* by *construction*).
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: It reached **1.0** in 2015, and it is now the *language* that *governments* and *operating-system* *projects* (including a *large* part of the *modernization* of *Windows* and *Linux* *drivers*) are *choosing* for *new* *safety-critical* *systems* \cite{rust_lang}.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: The *psychology* of Rust is the *psychology* of the *safety* *engineer*: the *goal* is not *expressiveness*, it is *the absence of a whole class of catastrophic failures*, and the *price* (a *steep* *learning* *curve*, a *compiler* that *argues* with you) is *worth it*.
statements.section: The Modern Languages (1990s–now): The Polyglot Era

statements.quote: In **1976**, **Stuart Feldman** at Bell Labs wrote **`make`**, a *tool* that *answers* the *question* “*what* *needs* to be *rebuilt*?” \cite{gnu_make}.
