statements.section: Version Control: The “Team” That Never Collides (1972–2005)

statements.quote: The *joke* is *typical* of the *open-source* *ethos*: the *tool* is *named* after the *user's* *imperfection* (the *bug*, the *mistake*, the *foolish* *commit*), because the *whole* *point* of the *system* is that *everyone* *makes* *mistakes*, and the *system* *exists* to make the *mistakes* *reversible* and *visible*.
statements.section: Version Control: The “Team” That Never Collides (1972–2005)

statements.quote: A *version* *control* *system* is, in *effect*, a *machine* for *forgiving* *human* *error*, and that is *exactly* the *role* that *software* — the *whole* *stack* of it — has *always* *played* in *relation* to the *human* *who uses it*: it *absorbs* the *error*, it *keeps* the *record*, it *lets* the *human* *try again*.
statements.section: Version Control: The “Team” That Never Collides (1972–2005)

statements.quote: Pull the *threads* together, and a *clear* *answer* emerges to the *question* the [Intro](intro) *posed*: *what* had to be *true* about the *world*, and about *human* *society*, before a *machine* could *learn* to *write*?
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: First, the *machine* had to be *cheap* *enough* to be *shared* and *many* (the *transistor*, the *microprocessor*), and *fast* *enough* to be *useful* (Moore's Law, the *GPU*).
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: Second, the *machine* had to *manage itself* (the *operating system*), so that a *human* did not have to *babysit* it.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: Third, the *human* had to be able to *talk* to it in a *language* that was *close to the problem*, not close to the *wires* (the *high-level* language), and to *share* and *reuse* the *answers* (the *library*, the *framework*).
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: Fourth, a *team* had to be able to *build* and *keep* a *system* *large* *enough* to be *smart* (the *compiler*, `make`, *version* control).
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: And *fifth* — and this is the *one* that is *easiest* to *forget* — the *idea* had to exist, *before* the *technology* caught up, that the *computer* is a *tool for extending the human mind*, not a *calculator*: the *idea* that was *stated* by **Licklider** in **“Man–Computer Symbiosis”** (1960) \cite{licklider}, by **McCarthy** in *1959*, by **Kay** in the *Dynabook* in *1968*, and by *a* *hundred* *other* *minds* in the *intervening* years.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: The *operating system*, the *language*, the *toolchain*: these are the *displaced* *prerequisites* of *AI*, in exactly the *sense* of the [Untold History](untold_history_i) chapter.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: They were *built* to *solve* *problems* that had *nothing* to do with *intelligence* (scheduling a *factory*, translating a *notation*, keeping a *team* from *colliding*), and *yet* every *one* of them is a *load-bearing* *fact* of *modern* *machine* *learning*.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: Remove the *operating system* and there is no *way* to *run* a *model* on a *many-core* *machine*.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: Remove the *compiler* and there is no *way* to *turn* a *researcher's* *Python* into *GPU* *kernels*.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: Remove *version* control and there is no *way* for the *hundreds* of *people* who *build* a *frontier* *model* to *work* *together*.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: Remove the *language* and there is no *way* for a *scientist* to *prototype* an *idea*.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: The *stack* is *not* a *coincidence*; it is the *necessary* *scaffolding* on which the *model* *stands*.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: Margaret Hamilton, whose work on the Apollo flight software is one of the founding acts of *software engineering* as a discipline.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: Apollo AGC software modules.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: The flight software had to *detect and recover* from *errors* in *real time*, on a machine with *less memory than a modern calculator*.
statements.section: What Was Required, in the End, for a Human to Build Something Like Today's AI

statements.quote: The word **“software engineering”** was *coined* at the **1968** **Garmisch** conference (the *First International Conference on Software Engineering*), where the *participants* — many of them *watching* the *Apollo* program — agreed that *software* had grown *too* *large* and *too* *important* to be a *craft*, and that it needed to be an *engineering* *discipline*, with *methods*, *standards*, and *measures* \cite{garmisch1968}.
statements.section: “Software Engineering”: The Moment Software Became a *Discipline*

statements.quote: The *person* most *associated* with *making* that *idea* *real* is **Margaret Hamilton**, whose team wrote the **Apollo** *Guidance* *Computer*'s *flight* *software* — a *system* that had to *detect* its *own* *errors* and *recover*, *in flight*, on a machine with *less* memory than a *pocket* *calculator* \cite{chm}.
statements.section: “Software Engineering”: The Moment Software Became a *Discipline*

statements.quote: The *famous* *photograph* of *Hamilton* *standing* beside a *pyramid* of *punch* *cards* (the *entire* *Apollo* *AGC* *software*, *stacked*) is *one* of the *icons* of the *field*, and the *idea* it *embodies* — that *software* is a *serious*, *measurable*, *engineerable* *thing*, with *failure* *modes* that must be *designed* *against* — is the *idea* that *underlies* the *entire* *modern* *practice* of *building* *reliable* *large* *systems*, *including* the *training* and *deployment* of *large* *models*.
statements.section: “Software Engineering”: The Moment Software Became a *Discipline*

statements.quote: The *pyramid* *photo* is *often* *described* as showing “*72,000 lines of code in 72 kilobytes*,” and the *numbers* are *broadly* *right* in *spirit* if not in *detail*: the *Apollo* *AGC* *software* was *enormous* *for* its *hardware*, and *Hamilton's* *team* had to *invent* *most* of the *techniques* of *real-time*, *fault-tolerant*, *resource-constrained* *software* *from scratch*, because there *was no* *prior* *art* \cite{chm}.
statements.section: “Software Engineering”: The Moment Software Became a *Discipline*

statements.quote: The *deeper* *point* is *not* the *lines of code*; it is that *Hamilton* *treated* the *software* as a *first-class* *engineering* *artifact*, with a *name* (“*software* *engineering*”), a *method*, and a *standard of proof* (the *system* must *be* *able* to *prove* that it *will not* *fail* *in* a *way* that *kills* the *astronauts*).
statements.section: “Software Engineering”: The Moment Software Became a *Discipline*

statements.quote: That *attitude* — *that* the *code* is a *load-bearing* *structure*, and that *its* *correctness* is a *matter of* *life and death* — is the *attitude* that *modern* *AI* *safety* is *only now* *beginning* to *adopt*.
statements.section: “Software Engineering”: The Moment Software Became a *Discipline*

statements.quote: The *technical* history — the *OSes*, the *languages*, the *tools* — is the *skeleton*.
statements.section: The Ideas and the Minds: The Geist of the Software

statements.quote: The *flesh* is the *history of the ideas* and the *psychology of the people* who *fought* over them, and it is the *part* that *explains* *why* the *stack* has the *shape* it *does*.
statements.section: The Ideas and the Minds: The Geist of the Software

statements.quote: Software is *defined* by its *arguments*.
statements.section: The Great Arguments

statements.quote: There is no *area* of it in which the *right* *answer* was *obvious*, and the *shape* of the *modern* *stack* is the *shape of the* *arguments* that were *won* (or *left* *unresolved*).
statements.section: The Great Arguments

statements.quote: * **Monolithic versus microkernel.** *Should* the *kernel* be a *big* *monolith* (fast, but *hard* to *verify*) or a *small* *microkernel* (clean, but *slower*)?
statements.section: The Great Arguments

statements.quote: Fought by **Tanenbaum** and **Torvalds** (MINIX’s microkernel versus Linux’s monolith), *resolved* (in *practice*) by the *hybrid* \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Great Arguments

statements.quote: * **Top-down versus bottom-up.** *Should* you *design* the *whole* *system* *first* (the *Multics* *way*, the *comprehensive* *specification*) or *build* it *in* *small*, *composable* *pieces* (the *Unix* *way*, the *“do one thing well”*)?
statements.section: The Great Arguments

statements.quote: The *Unix* *way* *won* the *operating system* *war*, and it is the *way* that *most* *modern* *software* is *built* \cite{unix_ts}.
statements.section: The Great Arguments

statements.quote: * **Open versus closed.** *Should* the *code* be *free* to *read* and *modify* (the *Unix* *BSD* *camp*, the *free-software* *movement*, *open* *source*), or *proprietary* (the *System V* *camp*, the *commercial* *empire*)?
statements.section: The Great Arguments

statements.quote: The *answer* is *both*, in a *tension* that *has never* been *resolved* and that *defines* the *industry* \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Great Arguments

statements.quote: * **Purity versus pragmatism.** *Should* the *language* be *pure* and *provable* (the *functional* *camp*, *Haskell*) or *pragmatic* and *powerful* (the *systems* *camp*, *C* and *C++)*?
statements.section: The Great Arguments

statements.quote: The *answer* is *a* *spectrum*, and the *spectrum* is the *whole* *space* of *languages* \cite{haskell}.
statements.section: The Great Arguments

statements.quote: The *people* matter as *much* as the *ideas*, because the *ideas* were *carried* by *specific* *minds* with *specific* *temperaments*:
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: * **Dennis Ritchie** was the *quiet* *perfectionist*.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: He *built* *C* and *Unix* with a *minimalism* that was *almost* *aesthetic*: the *fewest* *keywords*, the *smallest* *kernel*, the *cleanest* *interface*.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: His *style* is the *style* of the *Unix* *philosophy* made *flesh* \cite{unix_ts}.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: * **Ken Thompson** was the *hacker* *for* *whom* the *work* was the *pleasure*.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: *“If it is not fun, it is not worth doing”* is *his* *creed*, and *Unix*, *Plan 9*, *Go* — all of it — is the *work* of a *man* who *built* *systems* because *building* *systems* was *fun* \cite{bell_labs}.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: * **Grace Hopper** was the *saleswoman* for the *idea* that the *machine* should *speak* *English*.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: She *built* the *first* *compiler*, but she *sold* the *idea* of *machine-independent* *programming* to a *world* that *did not* *believe* it *yet* \cite{chm}.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: * **John McCarthy** was the *logician* who *predicted* *machine* *intelligence* as a *matter of course*, in *1959*, and *built* the *language* (*Lisp*) in which that *prediction* was *first* *programmed* \cite{lispworks}.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: * **Alan Kay** was the *visionary* who *sketched* the *personal*, *graphical*, *learning* *computer* in *1968* and *built* a *prototype* of it in *1973*, *twenty* *years* before the *market* *was ready* \cite{smalltalk}.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: * **Bjarne Stroustrup** was the *pragmatist* who *refused* to *choose* between *power* and *convenience*, and *paid* for it in *complexity* \cite{isocpp}.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: * **Niklaus Wirth** was the *pedagogue* who *believed* that a *language* should be *small enough to be understood*, and who *built* *Pascal* to *prove* it \cite{pascal}.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: * **Richard Stallman** was the *ideologist* for whom the *freedom* of the *software* was the *point*, and who *built* the *GNU* *Hurd* as a *monument* to that *idea*, *whether* or not it *ever* *became* the *default* \cite{gnu_hurd}.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: * **Linus Torvalds** was the *pragmatist* *organizer* who *proved* that a *large* *system* (the *Linux* *kernel*, *Git*, and, through them, much of the *infrastructure* of *modern* *AI*) could be *built* by a *distributed*, *open*, *ruthlessly* *meritocratic* *team*, and who *named* his *tool* after the *user's* *foolishness* \cite{git}.
statements.section: The Psychology of the Builders

statements.quote: Running through all of this is a *distinctive* *psychology*, the **hacker ethic**: the *belief* that *information* should be *free*, that *software* should be *shared* and *improved* by *everyone*, that the *measure* of a *programmer* is the *quality* of the *work* (not the *title* or the *institution*), and that the *intrinsic* *pleasure* of *making a clever, working thing* is a *legitimate*, even *primary*, motivation \cite{bell_labs}.
statements.section: The Hacker Ethic and the Gift Economy

statements.quote: This *ethic* is the *engine* of the *open* *side* of *software*: of *Unix* (*given away* by *Bell Labs*), of *open source* (*Linux*, *Git*, *the* *web* *browser*), of *free* *software* (*GNU*, *the* *Hurd*), and — *directly* — of the *open* *model* *movement* in *AI* (*the* *open-weights* *models*, *the* *open* *frameworks*, *the* *public* *datasets*).
statements.section: The Hacker Ethic and the Gift Economy

statements.quote: The *hacker ethic* is the *cultural* *prerequisite* of *open* *AI*, in exactly the *way* that the *operating system* is the *technical* *prerequisite*: without the *belief* that *sharing* the *work* *makes* it *better*, there is no *open* *ecosystem*, and without the *open* *ecosystem*, the *pace* of *progress* in *AI* would have been *slower* by an *order* of *magnitude*.
statements.section: The Hacker Ethic and the Gift Economy

statements.quote: Look at the *whole* *ladder* again, from the *bottom* up, and the *shape* of it is *not* *accidental*.
statements.section: The Thread That Runs All the Way Down

statements.quote: It is the *shape* of the *idea* that **computation is the manipulation of symbols**, *stated* by **Leibniz**, *proved* by **Turing**, *built* by **Ritchie** and *the* *Unix* *group*, *expressed* in *a* *hundred* *languages*, *managed* by *a* *hundred* *operating* *systems*, and *finally* — *in* the *model* — *turned back on itself*: a *system* of *symbol* *manipulation* that *learns* *the* *rules* of *symbol* *manipulation* from *the* *data*, instead of *having them written down*.
statements.section: The Thread That Runs All the Way Down

statements.quote: The *operating system* *abstracts* the *machine*.
statements.section: The Thread That Runs All the Way Down

statements.quote: The *language* *abstracts* the *operating system*.
statements.section: The Thread That Runs All the Way Down

statements.quote: The *framework* *abstracts* the *language*.
statements.section: The Thread That Runs All the Way Down

statements.quote: The *model* *abstracts* the *data*.
statements.section: The Thread That Runs All the Way Down

statements.quote: And the *user* — the *human* who *types* a *sentence* into a *chat* *box* — is *abstracted* from *all* of it, *standing* at the *top* of the *ladder*, *speaking* to a *machine* in *the* *only* *language* that *has never* *needed* a *compiler*: *the* *human* *one*.
statements.section: The Thread That Runs All the Way Down

statements.quote: Every *rung* of the *ladder* was *built* by a *rival* *mind* who *believed* that *their* *abstraction* was the *right* *one*, and *the* *stack* is the *record* of *which* *abstractions* *survived* the *competition*.
statements.section: The Thread That Runs All the Way Down

statements.quote: That is the *deep* *lesson* of the *whole* *page*, and it is the *lesson* that *belongs* in the *mind* *chapter* alongside it: **without the competition, there is no ladder, and without the ladder, there is no AI.**
statements.section: The Thread That Runs All the Way Down
